findings.lesson_text: The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: "You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad – the struggle of a person against their own desires" (Hadith).
findings.issue: This hadith is widely considered weak or unauthentic by mainstream hadith scholars but is cited as plain "(Hadith)" with no qualification, implying canonical authority it does not hold.
findings.canonical_truth: The tradition does not appear in any of the six authoritative hadith collections (Kutub al-Sittah). Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani grades its chain of transmission as weak. The narration is traced to al-Khatib al-Baghdadi's 11th-century History of Baghdad, a biographical work, not a canonical hadith collection. The lesson's uncaveated citation misrepresents its scholarly status.

findings.lesson_text: The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: "You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad – the struggle of a person against their own desires" (Hadith).
findings.issue: Same content_html as Unity Jihad lesson. Weak/disputed hadith presented without qualification as authentic scripture.
findings.canonical_truth: This hadith is not in any of the six canonical collections. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani grades its chain of transmission as weak. It is traced to al-Khatib al-Baghdadi's History of Baghdad (11th century), not to Bukhari, Muslim, or any other authoritative collection. Presenting it as simply "(Hadith)" misrepresents its scholarly status to GCSE students.

findings.lesson_text: Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to "Read!" (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but the words were pressed into his heart.
findings.issue: The lesson conflates two separate elements of the first revelation: the physical pressing described in Sahih Bukhari 3 (Jibril squeezing the Prophet physically three times) with an inaccurate detail about words being pressed into his heart. The canonical hadith does not describe words being pressed into his heart.
findings.canonical_truth: Sahih Bukhari 3: Jibril caught the Prophet forcefully and pressed him hard three times, then commanded him to recite. The Prophet returned to Khadijah "with his heart beating severely" — but the canonical account does not say words were pressed into his heart. The command was oral: Jibril said "Recite" (iqra) and the Prophet repeated the words aloud. Additionally, Sahih International translates 96:1 as "Recite in the name of your Lord" not "Read."

findings.lesson_text: Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to "Read!" (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but the words were pressed into his heart.
findings.issue: Same content_html as AQA Risalah lesson. Conflation of the canonical physical pressing with a non-canonical detail about words being pressed into the heart.
findings.canonical_truth: Sahih Bukhari 3 describes three forceful physical embraces by Jibril followed by a verbal command to recite. There is no canonical basis for the claim that words were pressed into the Prophet's heart. The first revelation account is the same hadith referenced in AQA L3.

findings.lesson_title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah & Angels
findings.lesson_text: Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful... Surah 2:20 states: "Allah has power over everything."
findings.issue: Quran 2:20 is cited as a creedal affirmation of divine omnipotence, but the verse's primary context is a metaphor about hypocrites walking by lightning flashes and freezing in darkness. The omnipotence statement is the closing remark on that metaphor, not a direct doctrinal declaration. Presenting it as a standalone proof-text for Al-Qadir decontextualises it significantly.
findings.canonical_truth: Quran 2:20 (standard translation): "It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still. Had Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and sight. Surely Allah is Most Capable of everything." The verse is about hypocrites (2:17–20 context). More fitting omnipotence proof-texts include 2:284 or 3:26.

findings.lesson_title: Tawhid and the Nature of Allah
findings.lesson_text: Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful... Surah 2:20 states: "Allah has power over everything."
findings.issue: Same content_html as AQA Tawhid lesson. Verse 2:20 decontextualised from its primary meaning (a hypocrite metaphor) and presented as a direct creedal affirmation of omnipotence.
findings.canonical_truth: See finding for religious-studies-aqa islam-beliefs L2. The closing phrase of 2:20 is accurate but the verse's primary subject is hypocrites, not divine attributes.

findings.lesson_text: The Qur'an states: "He wants that you must complete the same number of days, and that you must magnify Allah for having guided you so that you may be grateful to Him" (2:185). This verse connects the completion of Ramadan fasting directly to the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.
findings.issue: The quotation of 2:185 is a non-standard partial rendering that omits the verse's main content (the command to fast in Ramadan and the accommodation for illness/travel). The lesson uses it to link the verse to Eid al-Fitr, but the verse is about Ramadan fasting obligations, not primarily about the Eid celebration.
findings.canonical_truth: Quran 2:185 (standard translation): "Ramadan is the month in which the Quran was revealed as a guide for humanity... So whoever is present this month, let them fast. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then let them fast an equal number of days after Ramadan... so that you may complete the prescribed period and proclaim the greatness of Allah for guiding you, and perhaps you will be grateful." The verse is about the fasting obligation and its concessions, not about Eid.

findings.lesson_text: The Qur'an says: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months" (Qur'an 97:3).
findings.issue: The translation epithet "Night of Power" for Laylat al-Qadr is a variant rendering. Sahih International and the current Quran.com default translate 97:3 as "The Night of Glory is better than a thousand months."
findings.canonical_truth: Quran 97:3 (Quran.com standard): "The Night of Glory is better than a thousand months." Other common translations include "Night of Decree" or "Night of Destiny." "Night of Power" is widely used in older UK GCSE textbooks and is not factually wrong — it is a translation variant. The factual content of the verse (value exceeding 1,000 months) is correctly stated.
